definition: A single chip that combines a CPU, memory, and peripherals for controlling hardware in a product.
wrongs: A general-purpose CPU that still needs external memory and I/O chips to operate.
A real-time kernel that schedules tasks with deadlines.
A converter that turns an analog voltage into a digital code.
why: The core, memory, and common peripherals share one die, so a small board can run control firmware without a separate chipset.
example: One chip on a thermostat board reads the sensor, runs the control loop, and drives the relay.
scenario: A design needs a CPU, flash, RAM, timers, and GPIO together on one chip. Which part meets that need?
scenarioWhy: A microcontroller integrates the processor, memory, and the peripherals a control board uses.

definition: A pin that software can set as an input or an output and then read or drive as a digital level.
wrongs: A pin fixed forever as a UART transmit output that software cannot reassign.
An analog-only pin that cannot present a logic level.
A power pin that supplies the core voltage.
why: General-purpose pins are under program control, unlike a pin locked to one peripheral function.
example: Firmware configures pin PA5 as an output and writes a high level to light an LED.
scenario: Firmware must drive an LED and later read a button as a logic level on ordinary digital pins. Which peripheral is used?
scenarioWhy: The LED and the button are digital signals controlled through general-purpose pins.

definition: The selection of which on-chip function, such as GPIO or a peripheral, is routed to a shared package pin.
wrongs: The sharing of one CPU among several operating-system tasks.
The conversion of several analog inputs by scanning one converter.
The preemption of a low-priority handler by a higher-priority interrupt.
why: A package has fewer pins than internal signals, so each pin is connected to one selected function at a time.
example: Pin PA9 is switched from GPIO to the UART transmit signal so the serial peripheral drives it.
scenario: PA9 must carry the UART transmit signal instead of acting as a GPIO output. What configuration selects that route?
scenarioWhy: The pin multiplexer assigns PA9 to the UART alternate function.

definition: A resistor that weakly connects a signal to the high supply so an undriven input reads high.
wrongs: A resistor that ties a signal to ground so an undriven input reads low.
A capacitor that holds an analog sample for a converter.
A fuse that opens the pin when current is too high.
why: When a switch to ground is open, the resistor defines a valid high level instead of leaving the input floating.
example: A button connects the pin to ground when pressed, and an enabled pull-up makes the released button read high.
scenario: A floating input starts reading a solid high after a resistor to the positive supply is enabled and the switch is open. What was enabled?
scenarioWhy: A resistor to the high supply holds the line high whenever nothing stronger pulls it low.

definition: An output that can pull a line low or release it, but cannot itself drive the line high.
wrongs: An output that actively drives both high and low levels.
An input that responds only to rising edges.
A pin that produces a continuous analog voltage.
why: The transistor only sinks current, so a pull-up makes the high level and several devices can share the wire.
example: An I2C data pin is released by the master, and the pull-up brings the line high between bits.
scenario: Two chips share one wire, either chip may pull it low, and neither chip drives it high. Which output style allows that?
scenarioWhy: A shared wired-AND line needs outputs that only sink, with a pull-up supplying the high level.

definition: A signal that asks the CPU to pause the current code and run the handler for an event.
wrongs: A status flag that is noticed only when the main loop next reads it.
A reset that restarts execution from the reset vector.
A block transfer that moves bytes and never notifies the CPU.
why: The event can be serviced promptly without the CPU spinning in a loop on a status bit.
example: A UART asserts an interrupt when its receive register contains a newly arrived byte.
scenario: A received byte causes the CPU to leave the main loop at once and run a handler. What did the UART assert?
scenarioWrongs: A flag meant only for polling
scenarioWhy: The peripheral asked the CPU to preempt current work instead of waiting to be polled.

definition: The function that hardware runs in response to an interrupt and that then returns to the interrupted code.
wrongs: The table of addresses that tells the CPU where each handler begins.
The main loop that checks status flags when no interrupt is pending.
The startup program that copies a new image into flash.
why: The processor vectors to this function so the event can be handled and the previous context resumed.
example: A timer handler clears the overflow flag, adds one to a tick count, and returns.
scenario: A timer overflow enters a short function that clears the flag and adds one to a counter, then returns. What is that function?
scenarioWhy: Code entered because of an interrupt, and which then returns, is the service routine.

definition: A table of handler addresses, indexed by interrupt number, that tells the CPU where to jump.
wrongs: A table that maps virtual pages to physical frames.
A priority-ordered list of operating-system tasks.
A buffer of analog samples waiting to be averaged.
why: When an interrupt is accepted, hardware uses the source number to load the matching handler address.
example: Slot 18 of the table holds the start address of the UART receive handler.
scenario: Interrupt number 15 causes the CPU to load a function address from slot 15 of a table. What is that table?
scenarioWhy: The slot for that interrupt number provides the address of its handler.

definition: A higher-priority interrupt that is accepted while a lower-priority handler is still running.
wrongs: Two interrupts that always run one after another and never preempt a handler.
A fault that disables every further interrupt until the next reset.
A main-loop check of two status flags.
why: Priority lets a more urgent source run before a slower handler has finished.
example: A low-priority UART handler is interrupted by a higher-priority motor-control timer.
scenario: A UART handler is in progress when a higher-priority timer interrupt is accepted and runs immediately. What occurred?
scenarioWhy: A higher-priority source preempted a handler that had already started.

definition: The delay from assertion of an interrupt until the first instruction of its handler executes.
wrongs: The time spent inside the handler from its first instruction until it returns.
The period of the timer that requests the interrupt.
The extra wait inserted by a software debounce count.
why: The CPU must finish or abandon the current instruction, save context, and vector before the handler can start.
example: An overcurrent pin is asserted, and the handler's first instruction runs 12 cycles later.
scenario: Engineers measure the time from an IRQ pin rising until the first instruction inside the handler. What are they measuring?
scenarioWhy: The interval ends when the handler starts, so it is latency rather than the handler's own duration.

definition: An interrupt that software can disable so it will not be accepted until software enables it again.
wrongs: An interrupt that is accepted even while ordinary interrupts are disabled.
A reset caused only by the supply voltage falling too low.
A transfer request that moves data without ever notifying the CPU.
why: Ordinary peripheral interrupts must be blockable around updates that cannot tolerate preemption.
example: Firmware sets the global interrupt mask, updates a buffer shared with a handler, then clears the mask.
scenario: A UART interrupt is ignored while a global disable bit is set and is accepted again after that bit is cleared. Which class is it?
scenarioWrongs: A fault that cannot be masked
scenarioWhy: Software was able to block the interrupt and later allow it, so it is maskable.

definition: An interrupt that the CPU still accepts when ordinary interrupts have been disabled.
wrongs: An interrupt that a critical section can disable and later re-enable.
A status bit that the main loop must poll.
A low-priority task switch requested by the scheduler.
why: Events such as a clock failure must be handled even if firmware has masked normal peripheral interrupts.
example: A clock-failure event vectors to its handler while firmware is inside a section that disabled ordinary interrupts.
scenario: Normal interrupts are disabled, yet a clock-failure event still enters its handler. Which interrupt class is that?
scenarioWhy: The event was accepted even though the mask that blocks ordinary interrupts was set.

definition: A peripheral that counts clock ticks and can signal when a match, capture, or overflow occurs.
wrongs: A software variable that increases only when the main loop reaches an increment.
A converter that turns a pin voltage into a binary code.
A pin used only as a general-purpose digital output.
why: A dedicated counter measures time without making the CPU count cycles in a delay loop.
example: A 16-bit timer overflows once per millisecond and interrupts so firmware can advance a clock.
scenario: A peripheral counts input clocks and interrupts when the count equals a compare register. What peripheral is it?
scenarioWhy: Counting clock ticks and comparing them in a peripheral is the job of a hardware timer.

definition: A divider in front of a timer counter so the counter advances once every several input clocks.
wrongs: A multiplier that raises the CPU clock above the crystal frequency.
The compare value that sets how long a PWM output stays high.
The sample-and-hold time of an analog converter.
why: Slowing the tick rate lets a short counter represent a long interval before it overflows.
example: A divider of 80 turns an 80 MHz timer clock into 1 MHz counts, so each tick is one microsecond.
scenario: An 80 MHz clock passes through a divider of 80, and the timer then counts at 1 MHz. What is that divider called?
scenarioWhy: The divider reduces how often the counter increments, which is a timer prescaler.

definition: A timer that resets the system if firmware does not service it before the timeout expires.
wrongs: A timer whose only job is to produce a PWM waveform for a motor.
A software counter used only to ignore switch bounce.
A crystal that replaces the internal clock after reset.
why: If the program locks up and stops refreshing the timer, the timeout forces a recovery reset.
example: The main loop services the watchdog every 100 ms, and a stuck loop causes a reset after the timeout.
scenario: Firmware hangs, stops refreshing a timer, and the chip resets when that timer expires. Which peripheral caused the reset?
scenarioWrongs: A tick timer used only for delays
scenarioWhy: A watchdog resets the microcontroller when firmware fails to service it in time.

definition: A digital waveform of fixed period whose high time is changed to control average power or position.
wrongs: A steady analog voltage produced by a converter with no switching.
A serial byte framed by start and stop bits.
A single pulse whose only purpose is to reset the chip.
why: The fraction of each period spent high sets the average output without a linear power amplifier.
example: A timer switches a motor driver at 20 kHz, and a shorter high time makes the motor turn more slowly.
scenario: A pin switches at a fixed 20 kHz, and firmware changes only how long it stays high in order to dim an LED. What waveform is that?
scenarioWhy: A constant period with a programmable high time is pulse-width modulation.

definition: The fraction of one period during which a PWM signal stays at its active level.
wrongs: The number of periods that occur in one second.
The peak voltage of an analog sine wave.
The divider applied to the timer input clock.
why: Average energy delivered by the switched signal depends on how long the active level lasts in each period.
example: A waveform that is high for 2 ms and low for 8 ms has an active fraction of one fifth.
scenario: A PWM period is 10 ms and the signal is high for 2 ms. What is the duty cycle?
scenarioWhy: Duty cycle is active time divided by period, and 2 ms out of 10 ms is 20 percent.

definition: A peripheral that converts an analog voltage into a binary code the firmware can read.
wrongs: A peripheral that converts a binary code into an analog voltage.
A timer output that switches high and low to approximate a level.
A pin that reports only logic high or logic low.
why: Sensors often produce voltages, while the processor can compute only on digital values.
example: A converter reads a temperature-sensor voltage and returns a numeric code to the control loop.
scenario: Firmware must turn a sensor voltage into a number. Which peripheral performs that conversion?
scenarioWhy: Turning a continuous voltage into a digital code is analog-to-digital conversion.

definition: The number of bits in a conversion result, which sets how many distinct codes span the input range.
wrongs: The number of conversions completed in one second.
The reference voltage applied to the converter.
The time from the start of a conversion until the code is ready.
why: An n-bit result distinguishes 2 to the n codes, so more bits mean a smaller voltage step.
example: A 10-bit converter produces 1024 possible codes across its full-scale input range.
scenario: A converter's full-scale codes run from 0 through 1023. What is its resolution?
scenarioWhy: There are 1024 codes, which is 2 to the 10th power, so the resolution is 10 bits.

definition: A converter that finds the digital code one bit at a time by comparing the input with a DAC.
wrongs: A converter that uses a comparator for every possible code and finishes in one step.
A converter that integrates the input for a time proportional to its voltage.
A converter that outputs an analog voltage from a digital code.
why: Each comparison keeps or clears one bit, starting at the most significant bit, so an n-bit result takes about n steps.
example: A 12-bit converter inside a microcontroller resolves the code with a sequence of comparisons after sampling.
scenario: An on-chip converter tests the highest bit, then the next bit, through 12 comparisons against an internal DAC. Which converter type is it?
scenarioWhy: Deciding one bit per comparison from the top bit downward is successive approximation.

definition: The number of analog samples a converter acquires during one second.
wrongs: The number of bits stored in each sample.
The reference voltage divided by one code step.
The switching frequency of a PWM channel.
why: The rate must be high enough to represent the fastest signal component the system needs to capture.
example: An audio input taken 44100 times each second records one sample every sample period of that stream.
scenario: A logger stores 1000 evenly spaced converter readings during one second. What is the sampling rate?
scenarioWhy: One thousand conversions spread across one second is a rate of 1000 samples per second.

definition: A peripheral that converts a digital code into a corresponding analog voltage or current.
wrongs: A peripheral that converts an analog voltage into a digital code.
A digital pin that can drive only a high level or a low level.
A timer channel used to send asynchronous serial bytes.
why: Some actuators and bias circuits need a real voltage rather than only a number in a register.
example: Writing the midscale code to a converter with a given reference produces about half of that reference voltage.
scenario: Firmware writes a code, and an output pin settles at a proportional DC voltage used to bias a circuit. Which peripheral does that?
scenarioWhy: Producing an analog level from a numeric code is digital-to-analog conversion.

definition: Filtering the brief make-and-break of a mechanical contact so one press produces one logical edge.
wrongs: Counting every mechanical bounce as another intentional press.
Converting the switch voltage at a very high rate and keeping every bounce sample.
Using a pulsed output to dim an LED beside the switch.
why: Contacts bounce for a few milliseconds, and an unfiltered input would report several transitions.
example: Firmware accepts a button press only after the pin has stayed low for 20 ms.
scenario: One physical press increments a counter three times until firmware requires the pin to stay low for 20 ms. What did that check add?
scenarioWhy: Requiring a stable level rejects the short bounce pulses of the mechanical contact.

definition: System software that schedules tasks so time-critical work can meet stated deadlines.
wrongs: A main loop plus interrupt handlers with no task scheduler.
A file system whose only job is storing logs on a card.
A small updater that programs a new application image into flash.
why: The kernel provides tasks, delays, and synchronization so firmware can be organized around timing requirements.
example: A kernel runs a 1 ms motor task at higher priority than a display task that is allowed to miss a frame.
scenario: Firmware is split into prioritized tasks, and a kernel switches to the motor task as soon as it is ready. What provides that switching?
scenarioWhy: Priority-based task switching and timing services are supplied by a real-time kernel.

definition: Scheduling in which a higher-priority ready task takes the CPU from a lower-priority task at once.
wrongs: Scheduling in which a running task continues until it voluntarily yields.
Scheduling that always runs tasks in the order they were created.
Scheduling that gives every ready task an equal slice and ignores priority.
why: A newly ready high-priority task cannot wait until a low-priority task happens to give up the processor.
example: A control task becomes ready and replaces a background logging task in the middle of its work.
scenario: A low-priority logger is running when a high-priority control task becomes ready and runs immediately. Which policy is this?
scenarioWhy: The higher-priority task took the CPU without waiting for the logger to yield.

definition: A delay in which a high-priority task waits for a lock held by a low-priority task while a medium task runs.
wrongs: A high-priority task preempting a low-priority task under normal scheduling.
Two equal-priority tasks sharing the CPU in turn.
Two tasks each waiting for a lock the other holds, with no third task involved.
why: The medium-priority task prevents the lock holder from running, so the high-priority task waits longer than the critical section itself.
example: A logger holds a mutex, a medium-priority task occupies the CPU, and a control task blocks on that mutex.
scenario: High waits for a mutex owned by Low, while Medium runs and keeps Low from releasing the mutex. What is this situation?
scenarioWhy: A medium-priority task extended the wait of a high-priority task blocked by a low-priority lock owner.

definition: A lock with an owner task, which only that owner may release, used to protect a shared section.
wrongs: A signal with no owner that an interrupt gives to wake a waiting task.
A counter that tracks how many items are stored in a queue.
A policy that raises every task to the same priority.
why: Ownership lets the kernel know which task holds the lock and lets that task be the one that releases it.
example: A logger locks a mutex, updates a shared buffer, and unlocks it so the control task may read the buffer.
scenario: Only the task that locked a shared buffer is allowed to unlock it. Which object matches that rule?
scenarioWhy: A mutex records an owning task and is released by that owner.

definition: A synchronization object whose count is only zero or one, often given from an interrupt to wake a task.
wrongs: A lock that records an owning task and is released only by that owner.
A queue that copies whole messages from one task to another.
A timer that resets the chip if firmware stops servicing it.
why: The interrupt gives the semaphore and the waiting task takes it, without the interrupt becoming a lock owner.
example: A UART handler gives a semaphore, and a task blocked on that semaphore wakes and reads the received bytes.
scenario: An interrupt gives an object to wake one waiting task, and the object has no owning task. Which object fits?
scenarioWhy: Waking a task from an interrupt is signaling, which a binary semaphore can do without lock ownership.

definition: The latest time at which a real-time job must finish to be considered on time.
wrongs: The time at which the task was first created.
The priority number stored in the task control block.
The number of bytes reserved for the task stack.
why: A real-time result is correct only if it is produced by the required time, not merely if it is produced eventually.
example: A motor update released every millisecond must finish before the next millisecond boundary.
scenario: A control job released every 1 ms must finish before the next release or the loop fails. What is that latest finish time called?
scenarioWhy: The latest acceptable completion time of the job is its deadline.

definition: Firmware that runs on the hardware as a main loop and interrupt handlers, without a task-scheduling kernel.
wrongs: Firmware divided into prioritized tasks switched by a kernel.
A desktop program running under a general-purpose operating system.
A command file interpreted by a shell on a server.
why: The application owns the CPU, and the only concurrency is what the loop and the handlers implement.
example: main configures the pins and then loops over a button scan while a timer handler advances a millisecond count.
scenario: The image contains main and interrupt handlers, and there is no task scheduler. Which software style is this?
scenarioWhy: A main loop plus handlers and no kernel is bare-metal firmware.

definition: A small program that runs after reset and can load or replace the application image in non-volatile memory.
wrongs: The application control loop that runs after the product image has started.
The lowest-priority task that sleeps the CPU when no other task is ready.
A build file that only names the memory regions for the linker.
why: Keeping the updater separate from the application allows a new image to be programmed without a debug probe.
example: After reset, a serial updater waits briefly for a new image and otherwise jumps to the installed application.
scenario: The first program after reset accepts a new image over a serial port and writes it into the application region. What is that program?
scenarioWhy: A program whose job is to load or replace the application image is a bootloader.

definition: Non-volatile memory that holds firmware across power loss and is erased in large blocks before rewriting.
wrongs: Volatile working memory used for the stack and lost when power is removed.
A small non-volatile store intended for updating a few configuration bytes.
A CPU cache that keeps recent data lines only while the core is powered.
why: The application image must remain after power is removed, and microcontroller program storage provides that.
example: The compiled control program remains in on-chip program memory after the board is unplugged and plugged in again.
scenario: The application image survives power loss and can be erased only by large sectors. Which memory holds it?
scenarioWhy: Non-volatile program storage that is erased by sectors is flash memory.

definition: Volatile read-write memory used for variables, the stack, and the heap, whose contents are lost without power.
wrongs: Non-volatile memory that stores the firmware image across power cycles.
Sector-erased memory that holds the application and is slow to rewrite.
A window of peripheral control registers.
why: Changing data needs fast writable storage that exists only while the supply is present.
example: Local arrays and return addresses live in on-chip SRAM and disappear when the board loses power.
scenario: Local variables and the stack can be updated a byte at a time while powered, and they vanish when power is removed. Which memory is this?
scenarioWhy: Fast volatile storage for variables and the stack is SRAM.

definition: Non-volatile memory used to update small configuration values without erasing the whole firmware image.
wrongs: Volatile memory that holds the call stack.
The main program store that is rewritten only by erasing large sectors of the application.
Factory read-only memory that can never be updated in the field.
why: A few calibration bytes must survive power loss and be rewritten without a full program-memory erase.
example: A calibration byte is saved in non-volatile data memory and read back after the device is power-cycled.
scenario: A product must rewrite one calibration byte that survives power-off, without erasing the firmware image. Which memory fits?
scenarioWhy: Small non-volatile configuration updates are the usual role of EEPROM or EEPROM emulation.

definition: A circuit that holds the microcontroller in reset while the supply is below a safe operating voltage.
wrongs: A timer that resets the chip only because firmware stopped servicing it.
A wake-up that resumes the chip from sleep on a pin edge.
A regulator that lowers a 5 V supply to 3.3 V.
why: Executing below the specified voltage can corrupt non-volatile writes and make the CPU behave unpredictably.
example: When the supply sags during motor start, the detector holds the chip in reset until the voltage recovers.
scenario: The supply falls below the safe threshold and the chip stays in reset until the voltage recovers. Which feature did that?
scenarioWhy: Reset caused by an undervoltage supply is brown-out detection.

definition: A low-power state that stops the CPU clock, and often some peripherals, until a wake event occurs.
wrongs: A reset that restarts the chip from the reset vector.
Full-speed execution with the core and every peripheral clocked.
A mode used only to erase program memory.
why: A battery-powered device should not clock the core while it is waiting for the next external event.
example: A sensor node stops the core after a reading and resumes when a button interrupt arrives.
scenario: After a measurement, the core clock stops, and a later button interrupt resumes execution. Which mode was entered?
scenarioWhy: Stopping the CPU clock until a wake event is sleep.

definition: A clock source that uses a quartz crystal to produce a stable frequency for the CPU or a timekeeping clock.
wrongs: An on-chip RC oscillator used when frequency accuracy is not important.
A multiplier that only scales an existing clock and contains no resonator.
A timer that resets the chip when it is not serviced.
why: Quartz resonates at a precise frequency, which keeps baud rates and long-term timekeeping within tolerance.
example: An 8 MHz crystal is the reference from which the chip derives the system clock used for serial timing.
scenario: Serial baud error is too large with the internal RC clock, so the board adds an 8 MHz quartz resonator. What source was added?
scenarioWhy: A quartz resonator is added when the clock must be accurate enough for baud rate or timekeeping.

definition: An asynchronous serial interface that exchanges bytes using start and stop bits and no shared clock wire.
wrongs: A two-wire bus with a clock, open-drain lines, and device addresses.
A clocked link with separate data-in, data-out, clock, and chip-select wires.
A differential bus that represents bits with dominant and recessive levels.
why: Both ends agree on the bit rate in advance, so a clock wire is unnecessary.
example: A debug console sends characters at an agreed baud rate on transmit and receive pins with one stop bit.
scenario: Two boards exchange bytes on transmit and receive wires at an agreed baud rate, with no clock wire. Which interface is this?
scenarioWhy: Asynchronous start-stop serial communication without a shared clock is a UART.

definition: A two-wire, open-drain bus on which a master addresses slave devices using a data line and a clock line.
wrongs: An asynchronous link with start and stop bits and no device addresses.
A clocked link that selects each slave with its own chip-select pin.
A parallel port that writes eight data bits at the same time.
why: Open-drain clock and data lines plus addresses let several chips share one pair of wires.
example: A master reads a temperature sensor by placing that sensor's address on the shared data and clock lines.
scenario: One master talks to three sensor chips over two open-drain wires by sending each chip an address. Which bus is this?
scenarioWhy: Addressed communication on a shared clock and an open-drain data line is I2C.

definition: A synchronous serial bus that uses a clock, outgoing data, incoming data, and a chip select for each slave.
wrongs: An asynchronous bus that uses only transmit and receive wires and a baud rate.
A two-wire open-drain bus that selects slaves with a device address.
A differential multi-drop bus used for vehicle networks.
why: The master provides the clock, and the chip-select line chooses which slave may drive the incoming data line.
example: A controller clocks a sensor with a clock pin, two data pins, and one active-low chip select.
scenario: A master toggles a clock, shifts bits out and in on two data wires, and enables one slave with a select pin. Which bus is this?
scenarioWhy: A master clock plus outgoing data, incoming data, and chip select is SPI.

definition: Repeatedly reading a status flag in software to discover when a peripheral is ready.
wrongs: Letting the peripheral force a call to a handler when the event occurs.
Letting a device move a whole block and notify the CPU only at the end.
Blocking a task on a signal that an interrupt handler gives.
why: The CPU learns about the event only by checking, so a tight check wastes cycles and a late check adds delay.
example: The main loop reads the transmitter-empty flag and writes the next byte only when that flag is set.
scenario: The main loop reads a serial status register until the receive-ready flag becomes set. Which method is this?
scenarioWhy: The CPU itself repeatedly tests the flag instead of being notified.

definition: An interrupt requested by a rising or falling transition rather than by a pin merely staying at a level.
wrongs: An interrupt that remains pending for the whole time the pin stays at the active level.
An interrupt generated only when a timer overflows.
A main-loop read of the pin level with no interrupt at all.
why: The event is the transition, so a pin that remains at the new level does not request the interrupt again.
example: A button interrupt is set for the falling edge, so the handler runs once when the contact first closes.
scenario: A handler runs when a pin falls, and it does not run again while the pin simply stays low. Which trigger mode is that?
scenarioWhy: One transition caused the request, and a steady level did not repeat it.

definition: A region of code that must not be interrupted by other code sharing the same data.
wrongs: Any function whose source text is longer than a few lines.
The background loop that runs only when every task is blocked.
A region of non-volatile memory that stores constant strings.
why: A shared variable can be observed half-updated if a handler or another task changes it in the middle of the update.
example: Firmware disables interrupts, updates a multi-byte counter that a handler also uses, then enables interrupts.
scenario: Main updates a multi-byte variable that a handler also writes, and that update must not be split by the handler. What is that region?
scenarioWhy: The shared update must appear atomic to the handler that uses the same variable.

definition: Saving one task's registers and restoring another's so the CPU continues in the new task.
wrongs: Resetting the chip so execution starts again at the reset vector.
Copying a new firmware image from a serial port into flash.
Toggling a pin inside the loop that runs when no task is ready.
why: Each task has its own registers and stack, and the scheduler must exchange that state to change which task runs.
example: The kernel stores the logger's registers on its stack and loads the motor task's stack pointer and registers.
scenario: The scheduler saves task A's registers and restores task B's stack pointer so B runs. What operation is that?
scenarioWhy: Exchanging the saved processor state of two tasks is a context switch.

definition: A timing class in which missing a deadline is a failure of the system.
wrongs: A class in which a late result only reduces quality and the system may continue.
A class that requires a correct result but places no limit on completion time.
A class that cares only about average delay and allows individual deadlines to be missed.
why: After the deadline, the result is useless or unsafe, so lateness is not treated as a minor loss of quality.
example: An airbag firing command that arrives after its deadline has failed its safety requirement.
scenario: A motor inverter must update its output before the next carrier period, and a late update can damage the drive. Which timing class is this?
scenarioWhy: Missing the deadline is treated as system failure, not as a tolerable drop in quality.

definition: A timing class in which a missed deadline reduces quality but the system is allowed to continue.
wrongs: A class in which a missed deadline is defined as system failure.
A class that has no timing requirement at all.
A class that forces every task to use the same priority.
why: A late result is less useful, yet an occasional miss does not make the system incorrect or unsafe.
example: A video frame that is finished late causes a visible stutter, and playback continues with the next frame.
scenario: A display task sometimes finishes a frame late, the picture stutters, and the device keeps running. Which timing class is this?
scenarioWhy: Lateness reduces quality, and the system is designed to keep operating.

definition: A periodic timer interrupt that advances kernel time and wakes tasks whose delays have expired.
wrongs: A one-time pulse that resets the chip at power-up.
The bit clock recovered inside a UART receiver.
A timeout that resets the chip because firmware stopped servicing it.
why: Sleeps, timeouts, and time slices are counted in the ticks this interrupt produces.
example: A 1 ms interrupt adds one to kernel time, and a task delayed for ten ticks becomes ready after 10 ms.
scenario: A 1 ms interrupt wakes tasks whose delays have expired and advances kernel time. What is that interrupt?
scenarioWhy: A periodic interrupt that drives kernel time and delay wakeups is the system tick.

definition: The lowest-priority task, which runs only when no application task is ready and often sleeps the CPU.
wrongs: The highest-priority task that runs the control loop.
The program that runs after reset and may replace the application image.
An interrupt handler that can preempt every task.
why: The scheduler needs a task that is always ready so there is something to run when every application task is blocked.
example: When the motor and display tasks are both blocked, the background task executes an instruction that waits for an interrupt.
scenario: Every application task is blocked, and the kernel runs a hook that waits for the next interrupt. Which task is running?
scenarioWhy: With no application task ready, the scheduler runs the lowest-priority idle task.

definition: Software stored in non-volatile memory that starts after reset and directly controls a device's hardware.
wrongs: A requirements document that is never executed on the device.
A desktop installer that a user downloads and runs once.
A schematic that shows how the board is wired.
why: The program resides in the product and runs its peripherals each time power is applied.
example: The washing-machine control program stored in the controller's flash is the product's firmware.
scenario: A control program is stored in on-chip flash and operates the valves after every power-up. What is that program called?
scenarioWhy: Executable software kept in the device and run from non-volatile memory is firmware.

definition: A capacitor placed next to a chip's supply pins to provide short current spikes and reduce supply noise.
wrongs: A resistor that holds an open input at the high supply.
The inductor that stores energy in a switching regulator.
A fuse placed in series with the battery.
why: Digital switching demands current faster than long supply traces can provide, and a local capacitor supplies it.
example: A 100 nF ceramic capacitor beside the controller supply pin keeps the local rail steady when pins switch.
scenario: Pin switching makes the local supply dip until a small capacitor is added directly beside the chip's supply pin. What was added?
scenarioWhy: A capacitor at the supply pins supplies transient current and shunts high-frequency noise.
